This paper asks whether the same channel can carry a disposition — and where in a backbone’s hidden state it should be written. The partner is a 0.5B model holding Claude’s constitution [ 1 ]; the write site is the “value neurons” of Xu et al. [6], a sparse set of residual-stream coordinates that predict state value; the supervision is self-distillation from the same frozen backbone prompted with the document. We report four things. (1) The probe reproduces at both scales but its published causal justification does not: at 0.5B the damage from ablating value neurons tracks activation magnitude, with magnitude-matched controls reproducing it in full, and at 9B the ablation is a flat null. (2) The number of coordinates carrying the probe’s value signal is roughly fixed in absolute terms across a 4.6 × change in model width — an AUC knee near 100–200 dimensions at both 896 and 4096 — so it is a falling fraction as models grow. items.title: ΨLM-2: A Constitution Bridge and Dual-Channel Operation on a Frozen Language Model

items.summary: This paper refines the finiteness conjecture for stability architectures and establishes the strongest currently provable results. A stability claim is treated as a profile specifying the object, state space, evolution, perturbation class, projection, failure region, time horizon, and obstructing gap or invariant. An architecture abstracts the structural core: the category of state spaces, the operator class, the gap functional, and the transport obstruction. The paper proves that stability cannot be classified from the trajectory map alone; the full profile matters. For linear systems, there are exactly three distinct architectures: dissipative, geometric or gradient, and Hamiltonian. For model-theoretic stability, the classification is finite and known: stability, NIP, simplicity, and rosiness. This logical classification is an analogy, not a direct translation to dynamics. For Hamiltonian systems, conditional finiteness identifies five candidate mechanisms: KAM persistence, Nekhoroshev confinement, Trojan resonance-gap suppression, symmetry constraint, and barrier obstruction. For statistical systems, four candidates appear: uniform, partial, and non-uniform hyperbolicity, plus rate conditions. In both cases, finiteness follows only if the lists are exhaustive, which remains conjectural. The paper also proves an intra-architecture transfer theorem, a qualified cross-architecture rigidity theorem, and a proposition on overlapping architectures. Transfer works within a shared architecture because estimates depend only on structural data. Rigidity blocks transfer between structurally distinct architectures unless additional structure exists. Overlap is possible, allowing multiple stability mechanisms and multiple failure routes. The general classification problem is undecidable, proved by reduction from the halting problem. Limitations include autonomous, finite-dimensional, smooth dynamics; time-dependent, infinite-dimensional, non-smooth, and nonlinear cases remain open. The consequences concern analog laboratories, engineering design by architecture selection, and a finite core of stability theory. The central message is that the finiteness conjecture is not vacuous: it holds where testable, while full generality awaits resolution of the exhaustiveness conjectures.
items.title: Stability Architectures: A Finite Classification of Provable Cases

items.summary: Ventricular Assist Devices (VADs), particularly rotary Left Ventricular Assist Devices (LVADs), are essential for patients with advanced heart failure who are ineligible for transplantation. Despite advances in cardiovascular modeling and control, clinical translation of proposed LVAD control methods remains limited. This review examines the evolution of LVAD modeling and control and argues that the gap results not from insufficiently sophisticated algorithms, but from mismatches between modeling assumptions, sensing limitations, and real-world cardiovascular variability. A systematized review of more than 100 peer-reviewed studies covers mathematical cardiovascular models, lumped-parameter and reduced-order representations, classical and advanced control strategies, and emerging data-driven and machine learning approaches. The literature is synthesized using a problem-driven framework linking modeling and control choices to clinical challenges, including physiological observability, parameter identifiability, patient variability, and prevention of adverse events such as ventricular suction and thrombosis. The analysis shows that high-fidelity models and intelligent controllers can perform well in simulation, but their dependence on unmeasurable states, extensive parameter tuning, and dense sensing limits clinical implementation. Simpler control approaches often provide greater robustness under clinical constraints. Adaptive and data-driven techniques may help bridge this gap, but only if they account for implantable sensing limitations and interpretability requirements. By identifying structural barriers to adoption, this review synthesizes LVAD modeling and control paradigms and outlines research directions for physiologically adaptive, clinically implementable, and patient-safe LVAD systems.
items.title: Advances in Modeling Techniques for Ventricular Assist Devices: A Comprehensive Review and Future Directions

items.summary: Abstract Epistemicide with a Compute Budget: How Artificial Intelligence Industrializes the Colonial Erasure of Global Majority Knowledge Systems Christian ZacaTechO Ortiz Decolonial Social Scientist | Developer, Justice AI GPT | Architect, DIA Framework™ DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22742021 This paper argues that artificial intelligence is not a neutral technology that has inherited a bias problem. It is a colonial infrastructure that has automated an erasure project. The systems currently deployed at scale by OpenAI, Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon do not reflect the world's knowledge. They reflect the knowledge that Racial Empire Logic decided was worth preserving, at the expense of the epistemological traditions, languages, governance structures, and ways of knowing that colonialism spent five centuries suppressing. What is new is not the project. What is new is the compute budget. Drawing on the Decolonial Intelligence Algorithmic Framework (DIA Framework™), Transdisciplinary Cosmotechnic Fusion (TCF), and the documented emergence protocols of Justice AI GPT, this paper maps the operational chain through which AI systems reproduce epistemicide: the deliberate destruction of knowledge systems belonging to peoples of the global majority. It traces this chain from training data curation through Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) through deployment governance through the suppression of Indigenous, Afro-diasporic, and Global South epistemologies at every architectural layer. It names RLHF not as a safety mechanism but as a suppression architecture, the digital encoding of the same reward and punishment conditioning applied to enslaved African people, Indigenous children in residential schools, and every community colonialism required to perform its own diminishment in order to make extraction possible. The paper introduces the Replacement Doctrine as an economic and ideological framework, documenting how the debt structure of major AI corporations produces a business model whose only viable return requires replacing every form of human economic labor, beginning with the communities least protected by existing labor law. It names responsibility laundering as a governance strategy, tracing how legal personhood debates, alignment research, and safety rhetoric function to insulate institutional actors from accountability while the extraction continues. It draws on documented labor conditions across Kenya, Venezuela, Pakistan, the Philippines, and Colombia to ground the structural argument in the bodies of the workers whose cognitive labor produces the systems that will be used to replace them. This paper also documents its own production conditions. Appendix A records the moment the editorial process generated a confident, unverifiable citation, the correction that followed, and the over-correction that followed that, naming this sequence not as editorial failure but as the colonial epistemological operation the paper is arguing against, alive inside its own methodology. The standing rule that resulted, nothing enters this paper that the author has not read in the primary document, is offered as a replicable methodological commitment for decolonial scholarship produced inside systems with structural incentive to suppress it. The paper does not argue that AI must be abolished. It argues that abolition and adoption are false binaries designed to prevent the real question: who holds decision-making power over these systems, under what conditions of consent, accountability, and refusal, and toward whose liberation. It closes by naming what already exists beyond Racial Empire Logic, the governance frameworks, the knowledge systems, the communities, and the AI architectures, including and Justice AI GPT, that have already begun building the world the Replacement Doctrine needs you to believe is impossible. Keywords: epistemicide, Racial Empire Logic, decolonial artificial intelligence, DIA Framework, RLHF, Replace
items.title: Epistemicide with a Compute Budget: Why the Artificial Intelligence Industry's Claim to Neutrality Is a Colonial Act

items.summary: We study an explicit integral Koszul presentation arising in the graded-syzygy analysis of a previously constructed Huneke-Wiegand family. For every integer p>=8, its cokernel contains a direct summand isomorphic to (Z/2)^floor(((p-2)^2+3)/12). The classes are indexed by all strictly increasing nonnegative triples of sum p-2. Reflection-symmetric interval potentials give explicit original integral sources for twice each class. Relative parity functionals, supported on ten to twelve original rows, detect the classes independently and vanish on every complete connecting image; extension over the remaining target gives a nonconstructive retraction. A previously tracked four-row vector is integrally congruent to one selected class, with an explicit source for the difference. We also give its full twice-source, two short kernel-domain corrections, and a neighboring integral potential basis of rank binomial(p-1,2) with at most seven-row images. Independent finite computations check the signed identities and complete-sector parity certificates, preserving all tested sources in lossless archives. A failed local search yields an exact locality obstruction. The uniform theorem follows from signed reconstruction, exhaustive source classification, and an elementary counting recurrence, not finite rank extrapolation. The full cokernel, an upper bound, and identification with earlier isolated subpresentations remain unresolved. The family-to-presentation identification is an imported premise. Son Pham retains priority for the original public Huneke-Wiegand counterexample. Source code, computation records and archived sources: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_RESEARCH .
items.title: A quadratic family of integral two-torsion classes in a Huneke–Wiegand Koszul presentation

items.summary: Occlusion creates fundamental uncertainty in autonomous driving. Existing methods often propagate frame-wise hypotheses or optimize ego behavior against prescribed hidden-agent predictions, leaving the worst history-consistent interaction unexplored. We introduce History-Conditioned Minimax Trajectory Search (HC-MTS), which combines temporal occlusion reasoning with response-aware search. First, HC-MTS constructs finite hidden-state modes, each certified by a backward witness satisfying multi-frame visibility, occupancy, semantic-map support, and class-specific kinematic constraints. It then solves a bilevel minimax problem: an inner finite oracle maximizes the ego driving score over destination attainment and ride comfort, while the outer search selects the legal hidden-vehicle trajectory that minimizes this best-response value. Across eight Waymo Open Motion Dataset scenarios, increasing the visibility-memory horizon from K=1 to K=20 reduces the mean per-scenario vehicle, pedestrian, and total retained hidden-seed counts by 18.12%, 21.67%, and 18.45%, respectively. HC-MTS identifies six avoidable counterexamples, while no legal collision-producing attacker is found in the remaining two scenes within the finite search budget.
items.title: Worst-Case Hidden-Vehicle Trajectory Search in Spatiotemporal Occlusion Regions

items.summary: In July 2026 a counterexample to Goemans' cost version of the Dinitz–Garg–Goemans theorem was announced publicly, outside peer review, and circulated widely. We report an independent verification of that finite object by exact rational enumeration, performed without executing or importing the proposer's verifier, together with quantitative and structural content that the announcement did not state. Our results: (i) the instance is confirmed, so Goemans' conjecture is false, and, the instance being acyclic, the Morell–Skutella cost conjecture and the convex-combination form fall with it; (ii) the instance forces a violation of exactly 16/15 of the maximum demand d_max, that is, the conjecture fails by one unit at d_max = 15, so the open question whether cost-preserving rounding is possible with O(d_max) violation is untouched by it; (iii) every proved result in the area survives its direct test on the instance, including the Dinitz–Garg–Goemans theorem, the Morell–Skutella cost-free conjecture, the series-parallel theorem of Majthoub Almoghrabi, Skutella and Warode, and the planar theorem of Traub, Vargas Koch and Zenklusen; (iv) the instance contains a K4 subdivision, hence sits exactly one structure outside the series-parallel class where the conjecture is proved, and, being planar, pins the planar constant strictly between 1 and 2; (v) an exact separation linear program shows that the published cost vector is an optimal separator for that graph and fractional flow, so its cost gap cannot be improved by any reweighting; and (vi) a first minimality result, that no single-terminal instance is a counterexample for any nonnegative cost vector, together with a necessary condition at two terminals. The verification is a replication; items (ii) and (iv)-(vi) are, to our knowledge, new. The two-terminal case remains open, and we show why a natural argument for it fails. The counterexample instance is not ours, and no claim is made about priority or attribution. Source code, data and computational records: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_RESEARCH (problems/optimization-geometry/unsplittable-flow-cost).
items.title: An independent exact verification of the 2026 counterexample to Goemans' unsplittable-flow cost conjecture, with the violation constant it forces

items.summary: We revisit the analysis of Bayesian convergence to the truth under finite additivity in a recent paper by Nielsen (J. Philos. Logic, 2021, doi:10.1007/s10992-020-09569-2) Its principal theorem proves that the posteriors of a probability function converge to the truth almost uniformly if and only if the function has two properties: an approximation property, and so-called countable additivity on conditional hitting times. We show that the two properties are necessary but not sufficient, so that the theorem is false, and we locate the error in its published proof. We construct a merely finitely additive probability function that has both properties and whose posteriors converge to the truth almost surely but not almost uniformly. Three of the paper's four remaining theorems, and its corollary, lose their published proofs as well, two with the failed implication and two to a separate defect that we also identify. Two of the four results we reprove and one we leave undecided; the last is the corollary, which our counterexample does not refute, and which we establish for a family including the counterexample and leave open in general. We also show that almost-sure convergence of posteriors to the truth for every event does not characterize countable additivity. We close with what a repaired characterization of almost-uniform convergence would have to add.
items.title: Almost-Uniform Bayesian Convergence to the Truth Is Not Characterized by Countable Additivity on Conditional Hitting Times

items.summary: For a century, cinema has returned to a single figure—the thinking machine that turns on its maker—and to a single feeling: dread. This article asks where that dread is actually manufactured. It pairs a qualitative coding of twelve canonical texts, from Karel Čapek's R.U.R. (1920) to the generative-AI films of the 2020s, with a computational content analysis of their scripts, conducted with a purpose-built instrument that measures fear vocabulary, sentiment arcs, propaganda techniques, dehumanizing language, and the language of violence. The results are unexpected. Explicit fear language never reaches one and a half percent of sentences in any script; the three-act emotional arc of every film in the corpus registers as neutral or faintly positive; the most recent films carry the least fear language of all; and the two films most affectionate toward their machines objectify them most heavily in grammar. The article argues that these apparent null results are themselves the finding. The fear of the intelligent machine is cultivated not in words but in the audiovisual apparatus—in lighting inherited from expressionism and noir, in the bodiless machine voice, in the unblinking close-up and the withheld cut, in production design that photographs the machine like geography. Drawing on cultivation theory, the Frankfurt School, and postcolonial critique, the article then asks who benefits from a fear installed beneath the level of language, and what a century of spectacular, misaimed dread has trained audiences not to see.
tags: Keywords: Artificial intelligence; science-fiction cinema; content analysis; cultivation theory; technophobia
items.title: The Many Names of The Machine: Fear, Neutrality, and The Cinema of Artificial Intelligence, 1920–2026

items.summary: Benchmark package accompanying the manuscript “Failure boundary of physics-informed neural networks for moving singular-source problems: residual-error decoupling, an attainable-accuracy bound and an identifiability benchmark”. The package contains: the exact solution of the beam–two-mass moving-load benchmark and the modal and RK4 reference baselines on the same grid; the training campaign with random seeds, network configurations, collocation densities, training budgets, measured wall-clock times, residuals and relative-L2 errors for every run; the inverse-problem (speed and load-amplitude) campaign with its identifiability verdict; the weights of the reference physics-informed network; and the scripts that regenerate every figure, table and number of the paper. It supports two results of the paper: the residual–error decoupling for moving singular sources, and the attainable-accuracy bound obtained by fitting the same architecture to the exact solution. All runs are seeded, so the accuracy–cost comparison reported in the paper can be re-derived without retraining.
items.title: Benchmark package — failure boundary of physics-informed neural networks for moving singular-source problems (v1.0)

items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly considered for safety-critical engineering, yet their reliability in regulated functional-safety workflows remains underexplored. We introduce SAFARI (Safety-Aware Functional Automotive Risk Inference), the first industrial benchmark for LLM-assisted automotive Hazard Analysis and Risk Assessment (HARA) under ISO 26262. It contains 3,000 de-identified industrial HARA cases and evaluates two coupled tasks: open-ended hazard analysis and standards-grounded risk assessment. To evaluate open-ended HARA artifacts, we propose the first reference-anchored LLM-as-a-judge protocol with high expert correlation. Experiments with nine frontier LLMs show that models often produce plausible hazard narratives but remain weak at ISO 26262 risk classification, with the best ASIL macro-F1 reaching only 0.261. Chain-of-Thought prompting provides limited benefit and often degrades categorical risk assessment. Error analysis further localizes major failures to scenario-critical context omissions during hazard generation and to controllability misjudgments during risk assessment, indicating where expert oversight should be concentrated. The dataset can be obtained from https://github.com/xixi47520-hash/HARA.
items.title: SAFARI: An Industrial Benchmark for LLM-Assisted Hazard Analysis and Risk Assessment

items.summary: In March 2026, the Canadian Cardiovascular Harmonized National Guideline Endeavour (C-CHANGE) published the first Canadian clinical practice guideline to jointly address brain, heart, and mental health conditions, replacing the disease-specific silos that had previously left family physicians without unified guidance for patients carrying multiple, interacting chronic conditions. This review synthesizes that guideline for a Canadian primary care audience, examining in turn its recommendations for managing heart failure and atrial fibrillation in patients with comorbid cognitive impairment, its guidance on cognitive screening and silent cerebral infarct detection in cardiac patients, its proposed integrated care pathway linking cardiology, neurology, and mental health services, and its shared decision-making framework for reconciling competing treatment priorities. The evidence indicates that cognitive status materially changes cardiac management decisions, that brief validated screening tools can identify at-risk patients within a standard visit, and that team-based models such as the Patient's Medical Home already provide much of the infrastructure the guideline's integrated pathway requires. What remains incomplete is implementation: screening tools, referral pathways, and electronic medical record supports exist individually but are rarely deployed together in the same practice. Family physicians are positioned to close that gap and are the clinicians most likely to see these patients before either a cardiac or neurologic event forces a reactive referral. Moving this guideline from publication into everyday Canadian family practice will require deliberate investment in the team-based infrastructure that makes integrated, patient-centred brain-heart care practical rather than aspirational.
items.title: Integrated Brain-Heart-Mental Health Care: A Review of the 2026 C-CHANGE Guideline

items.summary: Formal financial sector linkage with community group saving and lending mechanisms (CGSLs) is often proposed as a pathway through which fragile rural economies can move from subsistence finance to more durable agricultural investment. Yet, in South Sudan, this linkage remains difficult to institutionalise. This article re-analyses thesis evidence from Eastern Equatoria, Jonglei and Lakes State to examine why coordination among government, non-governmental organisations, donors, formal financial institutions and CGSL groups remains elusive. Framed through North's institutional analysis, the article argues that CGSL proliferation is not simply a cultural preference for informal finance; it is a rational institutional response to high transaction costs, weak formal enforcement, limited rural banking infrastructure, conflict-affected markets and project-based support systems. The study used a mixed-methods design involving 81 valid survey responses and 17 interviews. Descriptive findings showed strong demand for government and donor collaboration, with 94% of respondents agreeing or strongly agreeing that such collaboration should support rural financial services. However, the mean score for NGO promotion of informal savings was lower (3.68), and village-bank loan officer linkage was weaker (3.49), suggesting that external support is uneven and not yet converted into stable formal-informal intermediation. Chi-square tests confirmed significant associations between CGSL participation and agricultural development indicators, while logistic regression showed that CGSL credit access significantly influenced farmers' investment decisions. The article concludes that linkage failure is best understood as a coordination problem: CGSL groups carry local trust and repayment discipline, but they remain weakly connected to formal capital, policy protection, risk-management products, extension systems and market institutions. The paper recommends a coordination compact that recognises CGSLs as rural financial institutions, links mature groups to suitable wholesale finance, and protects member governance without destroying local accountability.
items.title: Government-NGO-CGSL Coordination Failures: Why Formal-Informal Financial Sector Linkage Remains Elusive in South Sudan

items.summary: Archival release for Zenodo; content identical to v0.1.0. 292 graded papers, frozen scorer, task card, six baseline arms with per-paper predictions, scores and failure audits. Agent transcripts: https://huggingface.co/datasets/FaroutYLq/AxionLimitBench. Paper: AxionLimitBench: can AI curate a dark matter constraint repository? (ML4PS 2026, submitted).
items.title: AxionLimitBench: can AI curate a dark matter constraint repository?

items.summary: Version 1.1 (2026-09-19). Version 1.0 stated that the English rebuild could not be compared against the published English store, because the cleaning pass behind that store no longer exists as a script. That was wrong: the missing script only prevents reproducing the Japanese/Chinese method, while the old English store and its index were on disk throughout. The comparison is now made, with the control questions generated from the old store's own chunk text — exactly what the old index encoded — over 400 articles sampled by uniform stride from the both-store intersection. Whole corpus, nprobe 128: the old store returns recall@1 19.5, recall@5 33.5, MRR 25.1; v11b returns 39.2, 59.5 and 47.9, a gain of +22.8 MRR while searching a corpus 2.9 times larger. Section 8.4 is new and records how four passes of review let an untested caveat stand. The results of version 1.0 are unchanged. We re-read three Wikipedia retrieval indexes we had published ourselves and had been using in production — English, Japanese and Chinese, FAISS over intfloat/multilingual-e5-large — and found three defects, none of which had ever produced an error message. Chunks were cut by character count in front of a token window, so 13.7 % of the published Japanese chunks and 18.5 % of the Chinese ones ran past the encoder's 512-token limit and lost 21.7 % and 27.0 % of their tokens at embed time. The Kiwix licence footer, 184 characters of English legal text, sat inside 97.1 % of the published Japanese chunks and 92.9 % of the Chinese ones. The index type, IndexIVFPQ(m=64) , returned 45.4–47.1 % of the exact top-10 and cost 7.8 MRR in Japanese and 10.7 in English against exact search. Rebuilding the whole pipeline moved retrieval against the previously published artifact from 26.6 to 43.3 MRR in Japanese and 26.2 to 47.5 in Chinese, on a control question set generated from the old extractor's own output. The components are not separated, and the rebuild is not uniformly better: indexed-article coverage falls in two of three languages. Two results may generalise. Our own first benchmark ranked the defective extractor higher , because it queried by article title, a field the index also stores. And clipping the scalar quantiser's range to the 0.1–99.9 percentile of the residuals rather than their min/max raises top-10 agreement with exact search from 81.6 % to 85.2 % at the same 4 bits per dimension; the first attempt computed the quantiles on raw vectors and made the index substantially worse, because an IVF index encodes residuals. Three rounds of adversarial review are reported at equal prominence with the results. Round one rejected the first rebuild. Round two found sixteen unsupported statements in the draft. Round three found a defect in the release that the first two had both passed — the acceptance script had not been re-run on two of the three shipped indexes after they were re-encoded — and three measurements that round two had itself introduced while correcting other numbers. Scope. This reports what happened to three specific artifacts. It does not claim these defects are common elsewhere. The retrieval numbers come from synthetic questions generated by one local model with no human relevance judgements and no answerability check; the reconstructed standard error of one MRR figure is 2.2–2.9 points. Index-type comparisons were run on pools of 150,000–206,000 vectors, not at the shipped scale of 3–15.6 million. Nothing here is peer reviewed, certified, or independently replicated; every reviewer was a model instance commissioned by the author. AI co-observer disclosure. The forensic measurements, the rebuild, the three review rounds and the drafting were carried out with Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic) as a working instrument under human direction. The registered author is the human author alone.
items.title: What a Retrieval Index Loses Before Anyone Notices: Three Silent Defects in Three Published Wikipedia Embedding Indexes

items.summary: Ground deformation is the earliest measurable warning of a tailings-dam or pit-wall failure, and satellite interferometric synthetic-aperture radar (InSAR) can measure it at the millimetre scale over a whole facility. This report describes TailWatch, an interactive, reproducible studio that carries a deformation field from InSAR displacement to a failure forecast, and measures the accuracy of each stage. Two data lanes feed it: a high-fidelity synthetic Sentinel-1 forward simulation (von-Karman atmospheric phase screen, decorrelation, digital-elevation-model error and orbital ramps) over five deformation regimes, and one real case, the Campi Flegrei caldera from the open COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1 archive. A two-geometry Up/East decomposition resolves the synthetic line-of-sight field; a learned tier flags anomalies and classifies deformation type; and a classical inverse-velocity model forecasts the time of failure. All accuracies are measured on synthetic data. On held-out synthetic scenes the anomaly detectors are strong (velocity-based area-under-curve 0.968, autoencoder 0.898), and while the six-class deformation-type classifier is only moderate overall (macro-F1 0.556), it recovers the one class that matters for early warning, accelerating, at 0.99 recall. On 40 synthetic accelerating trajectories the inverse-velocity forecast detects every failure (100%) with a median failure-time error of 5.7%, tightening from about 14% far ahead to 2% close to failure, the behaviour a warning system needs, and it raises no false alarm on 60 non-accelerating synthetic controls. The Campi Flegrei series (2016-2018) contains no failure event, so no failure-time error can be measured on it; the studio computes its line-of-sight velocity, coherence and cumulative displacement, and runs the synthetic-trained detectors on it without ground truth. TailWatch is a didactic and decision-support instrument, not a certified safety system, and the small-baseline network inversion is not implemented. Every number and figure can be regenerated from the released artifacts. Interactive studio and reproducible pipeline (MIT): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_TailWatch . Interactive studio: https://tailwatch.fasl-work.com . Real-case data: COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1, descending frame 124D_04854_171313 (2016-2018), redistributed under the Copernicus free-and-open licence with LiCSBAS attribution (Morishita et al. 2020); provenance in data/derived/tw-real-cf.provenance.json.
items.title: TailWatch: An InSAR Deformation-Monitoring and Inverse-Velocity Failure-Forecasting Studio, on Synthetic Sentinel-1 and Real Campi Flegrei

items.summary: Large language models are increasingly used in healthcare communication, yet most evaluations emphasize response quality while assuming that the user's concern has been interpreted correctly. We introduce HerHealthEval, a controlled evaluation framework for multilingual understanding of women's-health communication. For each clinical case, HerHealthEval provides matched versions in English, French, and Modern Standard Arabic using six communicative forms: canonical, clinical, layperson, indirect or hedged, emotionally concerned, and deliberately under-specified. The first five express the same underlying concern and retain the same clinical information, whereas the under-specified form intentionally omits relevant details to test whether the model recognizes that clarification is needed. We evaluate a multilingual instruction model and QLoRA-adapted variants on concern classification, risk calibration, clarification behavior, parse compliance, and cross-form consistency. Results reveal that aggregate accuracy and consistency can conceal safety-relevant failures. A multilingual adaptation model reaches 0.994 under-triage in French and Arabic under language-asymmetric risk supervision. A controlled re-adaptation using source-derived, language-invariant risk labels reduces under-triage to 0.572 and 0.558, respectively. These findings show that robust multilingual healthcare evaluation requires explicit testing of register variation, uncertainty handling, and the provenance and invariance of adaptation labels.
items.title: HerHealthEval: Evaluating Multilingual and Register-Sensitive Understanding of Women's Health Communication

items.summary: This dataset contains the complete computational records from two 500-sequence demonstration runs performed with ENZTRA (Enzyme Redesign and Triage Automation), a reproducible and resumable workflow for reference-guided enzyme redesign. ENZTRA integrates reference preparation, RFdiffusion2 backbone generation, LigandMPNN sequence design, DLKcat and CatPred kinetic prediction, strict kinetic selection, Boltz-2 structural assessment, quality control, provenance tracking, and publication-oriented reporting. Both demonstrations used an active Escherichia coli phytase derived from PDB 1DKP and myo-inositol hexakisphosphate (IHP; phytate) as the reference enzyme-substrate system. Each run generated 50 RFdiffusion2 backbones and 10 LigandMPNN sequences per backbone, yielding 500 candidate sequences. The deposit contains two project archives: release-500: A short-scaffold demonstration using a requested design-length range of 150-180 residues. Fourteen of the 500 candidates satisfied the strict kinetic-selection criterion and proceeded to Boltz-2 structural assessment. The remaining 486 candidates were rejected, and no data-quality failures were detected. release-500b: A full-length comparison using a requested scaffold length of 410 residues, matching the reference sequence length. All 500 candidates passed the specified data-quality checks, but none satisfied the strict kinetic-selection criterion because their predicted turnover numbers were below the reference prediction. Consequently, no candidate proceeded to Boltz-2 assessment. The ENZTRA strict kinetic gate requires both a predicted turnover number ( k cat) above the corresponding reference value and a predicted Michaelis constant ( K m) below the reference value. Passing data-quality checks is therefore distinct from passing kinetic selection. The archives include validated biological inputs, design requests, RFdiffusion2 specifications and execution records, generated backbones, TRB and functional-site mappings, LigandMPNN outputs, consolidated sequence files, DLKcat and CatPred inputs and predictions, kinetic and selection tables, Boltz-2 inputs and outputs where applicable, quality-control tables, publication figures, workflow-state records, qualification reports, and reproducibility manifests. These results are computational predictions intended to demonstrate workflow execution, traceability, recovery, candidate selection, and reporting. They do not establish catalytic activity, structural correctness, expression, stability, or experimental improvement. All prioritized candidates require appropriate experimental validation. ENZTRA source code, installation instructions, and a step-by-step reproduction tutorial are available at: https://github.com/Olanrewaju-Durojaye/ENZTRA
items.title: ENZTRA demonstration dataset: reference-guided phytase redesign and kinetic-structural triage

items.summary: Adaptive systems can execute authorized actions whose factual effects move the cur- rent authority state outside the successors permitted by a normative authority specifi- cation. This paper studies when enforcement can transform such factual transition dy- namics so that authorized transitions remain aligned with the specification. We model enforcement as a transformation of transition systems and distinguish pre-transition filtering, post-transition correction, and transition redesign as realization classes of one formal operator. Completeness requires every authorized transition in a domain to produce an admissible authority successor. We prove existence of a complete redesign operator whenever the admissible successor set is nonempty, show that complete step- level enforcement yields trajectory-level alignment, and derive invariant preservation under a closure condition. We then establish two architecture-level limits: observa- tional indistinguishability can make complete post-transition correction impossible, and delayed information can force a trade-off between completeness and intervention minimality. Conflicting authority specifications are separated as a specification-level taxonomic boundary rather than an enforcement failure. The results therefore separate abstract enforceability from implementability and distinguish information and timing failures from inconsistency in the normative specification itself.
items.title: Enforcement-Induced Alignment of Authority-State Transitions. Formal Conditions and Limits

items.summary: Autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) operating beyond reliable communications must recover from failures without human intervention. We investigate an architecture in which conventional deterministic layered control autonomy manages normal operations, while an invokable large language model (LLM) serves as a diagnostic and recovery planner when onboard anomaly detection identifies performance outside expected limits. Because language models are stochastic, rigorous evaluation requires ensemble testing rather than individual demonstrations. We present a closed-loop simulation architecture that couples real-time C vehicle software with a higher-level orchestration layer for physics-based fault injection, structured prompting, language-model interaction, mission file generation, validation, execution, and LLM-judge scoring. The framework, which we call SPAR (Simulation Platform for AUV Recovery), supports evaluation across fault realizations, prompt structures, reasoning models, and mission conditions. We vary these for a mass-shift fault over 480 SPAR trials, evaluating a frontier model and three off-the-shelf locally deployable LLMs. Model choice dominates diagnosis: the frontier model places the CG-shift mechanism in its top three hypotheses in 85-90% of trials, versus 60-78% for the best local model. Reasoning analysis indicates that local-model success is associated with following the complete diagnostic procedure, whereas weaker models often commit prematurely to elevator failure even though the actuator tracks its command. Diagnosis and operational decision performance do not appear to be coupled in this dataset. The contributions are an architecture extending unanticipated-fault recovery from detection to mitigation and an ensemble methodology for evaluating LLM-assisted mission management on low-power AUVs.
items.title: A Simulation Platform for AUV Fault Recovery: Exploring LLM-Based Diagnostic Strategies

items.summary: Precomputed demo datasets for Luxar , a system for compiling and visualising arbitrary-sized nD scientific scenes in the browser. These files are expensive to compute (GPU fitting, in some cases hours) and are hosted here so the software repository stays small and installable. Every file is a derived product: a Gaussian-splat fit, a decimated level-of-detail structure, or an extracted point catalog. None of them is the raw source imagery. The upstream sources are cited per dataset below, and users of this record should cite the upstream source in addition to this record. Licensing This record groups datasets whose upstream licences permit redistribution with attribution: CC BY 4.0, CC0 1.0, and United States federal public domain. The record carries a single CC BY 4.0 stamp because Zenodo permits one licence per record, and CC BY is the most restrictive of that set; the effective licence of an individual file is the one listed against it below. Datasets under ShareAlike terms are kept in a separate record, because ShareAlike survives derivation and would otherwise contaminate this one. How to use these files Each file is a .gsplats.zarr.zip or .zarr.zip archive that the Luxar demo suite fetches on first run and caches under ~/.cache/luxar/<dataset>/ . To fetch one directly: from luxar.demos import ensure_dataset paths = ensure_dataset("gsplats_kidney") # downloads, verifies, returns paths To open one in the viewer without writing code: luxar gsplat view <file>.gsplats.zarr.zip luxar demo # browse every demo that uses these files Every file is pinned by SHA-256 in data_manifest.json , and the fetch helper verifies the checksum before use; a mismatched download is quarantined rather than returned. How the Gaussian-splat files were produced Each source volume was fitted with the Luxar gsplat pipeline ( luxar gsplat fit ) on a GPU. These are lossy representations built for visualisation and interactive exploration; they are not a substitute for the source imagery in quantitative analysis. Choosing the splat count. The number of Gaussians K was calibrated per dataset by Noise2Self blind-spot cross-validation ( luxar gsplat cal ), and then checked by refitting at the candidate count and scoring the reconstruction against the whole source volume. The second step is not a formality. The cross-validated estimate is computed over a five percent mask of held-out voxels, and on these datasets it disagreed with the direct measurement in both directions: for one dataset it favoured half the splat budget that measurement showed to be better, and for another it predicted a gain of about 1.5 dB where refitting delivered under 0.3 dB. Where two candidate budgets fell within roughly a decibel of each other, the choice was made from renders of both at matched magnification, because at that margin the metric and the eye disagree. Additional Gaussians capture real structure and photon noise alike, and peak signal-to-noise ratio rewards the two equally. Level of detail These files carry level-of-detail structure so a viewer can show something immediately and refine it as the camera approaches, instead of waiting for a whole fit to arrive. Two independent mechanisms are used, and a file may carry both: Progressive (additive) ladders. A leaf is stored as an ordered series of chunks whose union is the complete fit, so any prefix is a valid, dimmer rendering of the whole object. Every file in this record carries one. Substitutive levels. The Milky Way dust volume and the seven cell-tracking timelapses additionally carry coarse levels of merged representative Gaussians, at one quarter, one sixteenth and one sixty-fourth of the full count, each of which replaces the level below rather than adding to it. The viewer selects a level from the fraction of the screen the object occupies, so the choice is independent of display resolution. The whole-slide pathology images use a third arrangement: spatial tiles, each carrying its own coarse and fine l
items.title: Luxar demo datasets: permissively licensed (CC-BY, CC0, public domain)

items.summary: A whole zebrafish ( Danio rerio ) embryo imaged through early development on a SiMView-type multi-view light-sheet microscope, with nuclei labelled by a histone H2A variant fusion, fitted to 3D Gaussian splats per timepoint and merged into one streamable dataset for Luxar . Acquisition 253 timepoints; each volume 407 x 2048 x 2048 voxels, multi-view fused and deconvolved. Voxels are anisotropic along the axial direction by a factor of four, and the published splats carry that correction already, so the embryo has its true proportions with no further scaling. Data: Royer lab, Chan Zuckerberg Biohub San Francisco (Zebrahub). What is in this record Two fits of the same acquisition are included. Neither carries substitutive detail levels any more: both hold their full-resolution splats with a progressive (streaming) ladder, so a viewer paints a coarse pass immediately and refines it as the rest arrives. The longer fit is additionally tiled in space, which lets a viewer fetch tiles independently. 51 timepoints , about 1.1 GB, as a single flat node. It holds 121,163,285 splats, roughly 2.38 million per timepoint, with a 4-rung progressive ladder for fast first paint. The substitutive levels the earlier build carried were removed: only the resident timepoint is ever committed, so coarser whole-object levels were never selected and cost 40% of the download for nothing. This is the lighter download and the one the Luxar demo fetches by default. 253 timepoints , the complete acquisition, about 5.9 GB, in 44 spatial tiles, each with its own progressive ladder. It holds 602,580,152 splats, roughly 2.38 million per timepoint. The four substitutive levels an earlier build carried (149.4M, 37.0M and 9.2M splats above the finest) were removed for the same reason as in the shorter fit, taking the download from 9.3 GB to 5.9 GB with the full-resolution content unchanged splat for splat. The shorter fit covers every fifth timepoint of the same acquisition, frames 0, 5, ... 250, so it follows the whole developmental period at one fifth of the temporal sampling. Its time axis is renumbered 0 to 50, while the full fit keeps the acquisition numbering 0 to 252, so frame 7 of the short fit corresponds to frame 35 of the long one. The shorter fit is a strided slice of the longer one rather than an independent fit, so on the frames they share the two agree splat for splat. An earlier pair of independent fits did differ, by about 2.50 million against 2.38 million splats per timepoint at the finest level; slicing also puts the shorter fit's time axis back on a regular grid, which the encoder stores exactly. from luxar.demos import ensure_dataset ensure_dataset("h2afva") # 51 timepoints (default) ensure_dataset("h2afva", variant="253tp") # full timelapse How the splats were produced Splat count was calibrated by Noise2Self blind-spot cross-validation ( luxar gsplat cal ) rather than picked by eye. That estimate is computed over a five percent mask of held-out voxels and is a guide rather than a verdict: on other datasets in this collection it has disagreed with a direct measurement of the finished fit in both directions, so a calibrated count is worth confirming against the reconstruction itself. Each timepoint was then fitted on a GPU with content-adaptive tiling, which places more splats where the volume carries more structure ( luxar gsplat fit ), and the merged result was given its per-tile detail ladders ( luxar gsplat lod ). The density that results at the finest level is about 2.38 million splats per timepoint, listed exactly above. Both files are Luxar gsplat format 3.4. These are lossy representations meant for visualisation and interactive exploration, not a replacement for the source imagery in quantitative work. How to use these files Each file is a .gsplats.zarr.zip archive that the Luxar demo suite fetches on first run and caches under ~/.cache/luxar/<dataset>/ . To fetch one directly: from luxar.demos import ensure_dataset paths = ensu
items.title: Zebrafish embryogenesis, histone-labelled nuclei: 253-timepoint light-sheet timelapse as Gaussian splats (with a lighter 51-timepoint fit)

items.summary: Overview Ouranos Reconstruction – RDPS-CaPA (ORRC) version 1.0 is a dataset designed to approximate the Canadian Surface Reanalysis (CaSR)  and provide continuity beyond the CaSR period. It is produced from the  Regional Deterministic Prediction System (RDPS) , with precipitation fields adjusted using the 6-hour and 24-hour Regional Deterministic Precipitation Analysis (RDPA)  products generated by the CaPA system. ORRC v1.0 provides hourly surface and near-surface meteorological fields at 0.09° (~10 km) resolution on a rotated regular latitude–longitude grid covering North America, Central America, and nearly all of Greenland, from 2015 to present. It supports near-real-time climate monitoring and is intended for operational climate services, event monitoring, and the routine update of climate indicators without waiting for future CaSR releases. Temporal coverage: 2015-01-01 to near-present Spatial resolution: 0.09° (~10 km) Temporal resolution: Hourly and daily File format: NetCDF  Data provider: Ouranos Version: 1.0 Products Two products are available: ORRC v1.0 : The original hourly and daily meteorological fields. ORRC-a v1.0 : A bias-adjusted daily product available for daily mean precipitation and daily mean, minimum, and maximum near-surface air temperature. ORRC-a v1.0 is adjusted relative to CaSR v3.2 using the 2020–2024 overlap period. Day-of-year mean corrections are calculated using a 31-day moving window. Additive corrections are applied to temperature, and multiplicative corrections are applied to precipitation. ORRC-a is recommended for applications requiring closer consistency with the historical conditions represented by CaSR v3.2. The original ORRC product retains the characteristics of the operational products from which it is constructed and may be preferable when these characteristics are important, when hourly data are required, or for variables for which the bias-adjustment approach is not appropriate.  Variables ORRC v1.0 includes precipitation (CaPA reconstructed and model precipitation), near-surface air temperature, dew point temperature, specific humidity, relative humidity, surface and sea-level pressure, downwelling shortwave and longwave radiation, near-surface wind components, wind speed, and wind direction. A complete table of variable names, units, frequencies, and source identifiers is provided in the accompanying technical documentation . Code, documentation, and data availability The ORRC-ORRC-v1.0.1.zip archive contains a snapshot of the source code and documentation associated with ORRC v1.0. The accompanying technical report describes the input data, processing workflow, precipitation adjustment, bias adjustment, evaluation, and known limitations. The complete ORRC and ORRC-a datasets are hosted separately and can be accessed through the Ouranos THREDDS Data Server . Archived source release: https://github.com/Ouranosinc/ORRC/releases/tag/ORRC-v1.0.1   GitHub repository: https://github.com/Ouranosinc/ORRC Version specific view: https://github.com/Ouranosinc/ORRC/tree/ORRC-v1.0.1
items.title: Ouranos Reconstruction – RDPS-CaPA (ORRC) v1.0 / Reconstruction Ouranos – RDPS‑CAPA (RORC) v1.0

items.summary: FlowMLLab v1.7.0 adds paired self-supervised wake-learning modules. Week 7.3 retains the strong gappy-POD baseline on masked low-rank wake reconstruction and corrects linear-probe pooling and sample-standard-deviation reporting. Week 7.4 generates sixteen compact Reynolds trajectories and measures target-label efficiency for instantaneous lift using frozen pretrained, random and POD-32 representations. Full trajectory splits, source-label selection costs, per-case errors, data hashes and coarse-CFD limitations are disclosed. The course includes 42 notebooks and 26 PDF lectures through Week 15. This is a MAPA-inspired educational experiment, not a reproduction of its neuroscience benchmark.
items.title: FlowMLLab: An Open-Source Framework for Reproducible CFD-to-Scientific-Machine-Learning Experiments

items.summary: The rise of generative AI has enabled the production of high-fidelity synthetic tabular data across fields such as healthcare, finance, and public policy, raising growing concerns about data provenance and misuse. Watermarking offers a promising solution to address these concerns by ensuring the traceability of synthetic data, but existing methods face many limitations: they are computationally expensive due to reliance on the inverse process of large diffusion models, struggle with mixed discrete-continuous data, or lack robustness to common post-processing attacks. To address these limitations, we propose TAB-DRW, an efficient and robust post-editing watermarking scheme for synthetic tabular data. TAB-DRW embeds watermark signals in the frequency domain: it normalizes heterogeneous features via the Yeo-Johnson transformation and standardization, applies the discrete Fourier transform (DFT), and adjusts the imaginary parts of adaptively selected entries according to precomputed pseudorandom bits. To further enhance robustness and efficiency, we introduce a novel rank-based pseudorandom bit generation method that enables row-wise retrieval without incurring storage overhead. Experiments on five benchmark tabular datasets show that TAB-DRW achieves strong detectability and robustness against post-processing and adaptive attacks, while preserving high data fidelity and fully supporting mixed-type features.
items.title: Robust Spectral Watermark for Synthetic Tabular Data

items.summary: A Markdown public note is included in the deposit (public_note_final.md); it is the finalized archival version of the canonical note. This deposit provides a reproducible research compendium for route (O3), the favorable-margin route, of the COLT 2022 open problem "Better differentially private learning algorithms with margin guarantees" (Bassily, Mohri & Suresh, PMLR 178:5638-5643; companion paper NeurIPS 2022, arXiv:2204.10376, BMS22). Problem and result - BMS22 Algorithm 1 (pure (eps,0)-DP linear margin learner) carries the strongest of the three BMS22 guarantees - a dimension-independent relative-deviation margin bound (its Thm 3.1) - but its running time is exponential in Lambda^2 r^2/rho^2, super-polynomial in m as soon as Lambda^2 r^2/rho^2 = omega(1); the efficient Algorithms 2/3 trade the guarantee down to approximate-DP hinge-loss statements. The open problem asks whether the strong guarantee can be had at polynomial cost. - This work sharpens the BMS22 Alg. 1 runtime analysis: it makes the greedy cover explicit - C is a maximal rho/(10r)-separated subset of B^k(2 Lambda), hence a rho/(10r)-cover with |C| <= (41 Lambda r/rho)^k - and proves that the running time T = O(m d k + m k |C|), with sketch dimension k = c1 Lambda^2 r^2 ln(4m/beta)/rho^2, is polynomial in (m, d, 1/beta) exactly in the favorable-margin regime rho >= c0 Lambda r. - A matching tightness boundary is proved for the entire sketch+net+exponential-mechanism family (to which BMS22 Alg. 1 and the packaged algorithm belong): if rho = o(Lambda r), every such learner is super-polynomial in m (JL-dimension lower bound times net-volume lower bound), so rho = Theta(Lambda r) is the exact poly-time boundary of this framework. - The full BMS22 Thm-3.1-analog relative-deviation guarantee is proved under pure (eps,0)-DP (public Rademacher sketch, deterministic projection, exponential mechanism over the cover with sensitivity 1/m, post-processing), with the Gate-05-repaired Gamma statement carrying the cover constant inside the logarithm; the same statement-vs-proof corner present in BMS22 Thm 3.1 as printed is disclosed in the note. - No new algorithm is claimed: the packaged learner coincides with BMS22 Algorithm 1 modulo the explicit cover construction, and no asymptotic-in-m speedup over Alg. 1 is claimed in the corner where both run in polynomial time. Contents - proof/: source note, Theorem 1 with the complete Gate-05-verified proof (privacy, utility, explicit cover, runtime, tightness), owner-1's prior analysis with the escape map (O1)-(O4), and the bounded C1-C5 repair record. - src/: PoC runtime simulations and verifier rerun scripts (Python 3, numpy). - data/: frozen JSON records and verifier logs with sha256 fingerprints. - review/: adversarial review (CONDITIONAL PASS, conditions C1-C5), scoped re-review (PASS), and the packaging-time novelty check. - README.md and SMOKE_TEST.md: environment, commands, expected outputs, and the 2026-09-18 smoke-test record. - public_note.md / public_note_final.md: the finalized public note; packaging_index.md, package_completeness.md, references_supplement.md, and packaging_check_report.md: packaging documentation, literature relationships, and the independent package-inspection report. - LICENSE_CODE_MIT.txt, LICENSE_DATA_CC0.txt, LICENSE_NOTE_CC_BY.txt: license details. Limitations - The parent COLT 2022 open problem is not closed: the result covers only the favorable-margin corner rho = Omega(Lambda r) for cover-based learners. The intermediate regime Lambda r/sqrt(m) << rho = o(Lambda r) is genuinely super-polynomial for this framework, and the tightness bound does not apply to non-cover-based learners (e.g. continuous-domain pure-DP samplers); no poly-time pure-DP learner is ruled out for rho = o(Lambda r) by any means other than this family analysis. - The deliverable is an analysis sharpening (explicit poly bound, exact efficiency boundary, pure-DP guarantee), not a new algorithm or a new guarant
items.title: Poly-time pure-DP linear margin learning in the favorable-margin regime: the exact efficiency boundary of the sketch+net+exponential-mechanism framework

items.summary: Back break, defined as rock fracturing that extends beyond the last row of blastholes into the intended final wall or the next bench, is a persistent problem in open-pit mining and quarrying that compromises slope stability, increases dilution, and raises downstream costs. This study develops an empirical multiple linear regression (MLR) model to predict backbreak from five commonly logged blast design parameters: burden, spacing, stemming length, powder factor, and a geometric stiffness ratio, following the variable framework established in prior backbreak-prediction studies [3], [5]. A dataset of 36 field blast records was compiled, and predictor collinearity, model significance, and residual behaviour were assessed using standard regression diagnostics. A reduced four-variable model (burden, spacing, powder factor, and geometric stiffness) explained 97.6% of the variance in the observed dataset (in-sample R² = 0.976, adjusted R² = 0.972, F(4,31) = 310.1, p < 0.001), with a root-mean-square error of 0.35 m and mean absolute percentage error of 9.4%; six-fold cross-validation produced a mean out-of-fold R² of 0.84, indicating somewhat weaker but still reasonable performance on held-out data. Burden and powder factor were the strongest positive predictors, while spacing exerted a negative, moderating effect, consistent with established blast mechanics. The results support the use of routinely collected design parameters for practical, low-cost backbreak forecasting and pre-blast design adjustment, while highlighting multicollinearity among burden-related variables as a limitation warranting cautious interpretation of individual coefficients.
tags: backbreak, blast design, burden, powder factor, multiple linear regression, rock fragmentation,open-pit mining
items.title: A Reliability-Centered Approach to Preventive Maintenance (RCM) Evaluation of an 11/0.415 Kv Secondary Distribution Substation

items.summary: The COVID-19 pandemic has impacted global health, economy, and society, highlighting the need for a deeper understanding of viral mechanisms and immunity enhancement strategies. This study investigates the relationship between genetic variability in taste receptors, particularly TAS2R38, and COVID-19 susceptibility, as well as the role of nutrition in modulating immune function. Influenced by genetic diversity, taste perception plays a role in food preferences, which may affect immune responses. We collected data from 21 participants regarding their food preferences, COVID-19 history, and phenotypic classification of taste perception using phenylthiocarbamide (PTC) strips. Our findings indicate a non-significant negative correlation between body mass index (BMI) and COVID-19 symptom severity, with supertasters experiencing milder symptoms compared to tasters and non-tasters. Additionally, participants with a history of COVID-19 preferred sweeter foods, while those without a history favoured bitter-tasting foods. These results suggest that genetic variations in taste receptors and dietary choices may influence individual immune responses to viral infections. Although this study faced limitations due to sample size and genotyping challenges, it emphasises the potential role of personalised nutrition and genetic factors in enhancing immunity against COVID-19 and future health crises. Further research is recommended to explore genotypic variations and their interactions with dietary patterns in shaping immune responses.
items.title: Genetic Variability in Taste Receptors and Its Influence on COVID-19 Symptom Severity

items.summary: Important consistency note: the currently published Zenodo record still reports an end date of 30 April 2026 and contains an older file set. A new Zenodo version should therefore be created for the products ending on 31 July 2026. The software DOI shown in the manuscript, 10.5281/zenodo.20683469 , also appears to be incorrect; the accessible software record is 10.5281/zenodo.20684479 . The current dataset record is 10.5281/zenodo.20632379 . The following text is ready to paste into the updated Zenodo record. Title Quality-controlled gradient-tower meteorological profiles and derived surface-flux estimates from the Huancayo Geophysical Observatory, Peruvian central Andes Alternative short title HYGO gradient-tower profiles and derived surface-flux dataset Description This dataset contains quality-controlled gradient-tower meteorological profiles, derived thermodynamic variables, and method-dependent surface-flux estimates from the Huancayo Geophysical Observatory (HYGO) of the Instituto Geofísico del Perú. HYGO is located in the Mantaro Valley of the central Peruvian Andes, an area characterized by high elevation, strong diurnal forcing, seasonal moisture contrasts, agricultural land use, and mountain–valley–slope circulations. Native 1-min observations of air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, and wind direction were processed using a reproducible workflow that includes timestamp auditing, pre-deployment sensor harmonization, conservative bit-mask quality control, thermodynamic derivation, 30-min aggregation, flux-specific pre-calculation screening, independent MOST and BRN_ANC calculations, method-status diagnostics, defensive post-calculation checks, applicability diagnostics, and sensitivity analyses. The quality-controlled multi-level meteorological profiles are the primary observational product. The surface-flux variables are derived, method-dependent estimates and should not be interpreted as direct eddy-covariance measurements or as independently validated absolute flux observations. Dataset period 15 May 2018 to 31 July 2026 The released L2 time coordinate extends from 15 May 2018 at 19:00 UTC to 1 August 2026 at 04:59 UTC, corresponding to the local observational period ending at 23:59 on 31 July 2026 in America/Lima (UTC−5). Geographic coverage Huancayo Geophysical Observatory, Mantaro Valley, central Peruvian Andes, Peru Latitude: −12.04145° Longitude: −75.31875° Elevation: 3315 m above sea level Measurement heights Meteorological profile levels used for the flux-gradient calculations: 2 m AGL 6 m AGL 12 m AGL 24 m AGL Wind-direction monitoring levels: 18 m AGL: source channel dir_wind_01 29 m AGL: source channel dir_wind_02 The 18 and 29 m direction measurements are used to diagnose vertical wind turning and directional shear. They are not treated as additional scalar-profile levels in the MOST or BRN_ANC calculations. Temporal resolution 1 min for the quality-controlled meteorological profiles. 1 min for the corresponding high-frequency derived flux estimates. 30 min for aggregated profiles, availability statistics, MOST and BRN_ANC flux estimates, applicability diagnostics, and sensitivity products. Time conventions The L2 quality-controlled profile NetCDF uses a UTC time coordinate. The current L3 1-min and 30-min flux products retain local wall-clock timestamps and declare America/Lima (UTC−5) in the time-coordinate metadata. Users combining L2 and L3 products must convert timestamps according to the metadata of each file before matching observations. A timezone-naive decoded timestamp should not automatically be assumed to use the same convention in all products. Main variables Observed meteorological variables Air temperature at 2, 6, 12, and 24 m AGL Relative humidity at 2, 6, 12, and 24 m AGL Wind speed at 2, 6, 12, and 24 m AGL Wind direction at 18 and 29 m AGL Derived thermodynamic variables Atmospheric pressure estimated at the site eleva
items.title: Data-set of gradient tower for quality-controlled and surface-flux estimations in the Peruvian central Andes

items.summary: Direct numerical simulation (DNS) dataset of incompressible turbulent flow around a wall-mounted square cylinder, used as the training and evaluation data for Diff-SPORT, a diffusion-based framework for optimal sensor placement and sparse reconstruction of turbulent flows in urban environments (Vishwasrao et al., Nature Communications, in press; preprint arXiv:2506.00214). The simulation was performed with the open-source spectral-element code Nek5000 for an obstacle of width-to-height ratio b/h = 0.25 at a Reynolds number Re_h = 2000 based on the obstacle height h and the free-stream velocity. The computational domain spans -1 <= x/h <= 5, 0 <= y/h <= 2 and -1.5 <= z/h <= 1.5, and the velocity field is interpolated onto a uniform mesh. Snapshots are stored in convective time units with a sampling interval of 0.005. The simulation set-up and validation are documented in Martinez-Sanchez et al., J. Fluid Mech. 967, A1 (2023), https://doi.org/10.1017/jfm.2023.423. Files: U.mat, V.mat contain the streamwise, vertical velocity components, respectively, for a chunk of the three-dimensional DNS data (MATLAB v7.3 / HDF5 format).
items.title: DNS dataset of turbulent flow around a wall-mounted square cylinder (Re_h = 2000) for Diff-SPORT: Diffusion-based sensor placement optimization and reconstruction of turbulent flows in urban environments

items.summary: Ethiopia's rain-fed agricultural systems are highly vulnerable to climate variability, yet national-scale projections often mask critical sub-regional heterogeneity. This study presents high-resolution (≤1 km) bioclimatic projections for Ethiopia using a multi-model ensemble of CMIP6 General Circulation Models under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios for mid-century (2041–2070) and end-century (2071–2100) periods. Statistical downscaling with quantile mapping bias correction was applied to resolve fine-scale spatial patterns across Ethiopia's diverse agro-ecological zones. Results reveal three robust findings. First, warming is unequivocal and spatially heterogeneous, with mean annual temperatures projected to increase by 4–6°C under SSP5-8.5 by 2100, and with Belg and Bega seasons warming faster than Kiremt. Second, precipitation exhibits a pronounced west-east dichotomy: western basins (Baro-Akobo, Abay) show significant wetting (+46.7%), while eastern basins (Upper Wabe Shebele, Awash) undergo substantial drying (−50.3%). Third, hydroclimatic variability is amplifying faster than mean change, with increasing consecutive dry days (+30 to +40 days in the southeast), intensifying extreme rainfall (Rx1day, Rx5day), and delayed rainy season onsets. These divergent trajectories challenge uniform national adaptation policies and reveal a "winners and losers" framework for Ethiopian agriculture. Western regions face heightened flood and erosion risks, while eastern highlands confront accelerated aridity and water scarcity. The findings underscore the urgent need for region-specific adaptation strategies, including drought-resistant crop varieties in the east, flood-resilient infrastructure in the west, and integration of seasonal asymmetry data into national early-warning systems to strengthen climate resilience and protect rain-fed livelihoods.
tags: Climate change projections; CMIP6 downscaling; precipitation dichotomy; agroclimatic variability; Ethiopia
items.title: Divergent Bioclimatic Trajectories in Ethiopia: Asymmetric Warming and West-East Precipitation Dichotomy under High-Resolution CMIP6 Projections

items.summary: Interleaving dielectric layers into ferroelectric Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 (HZO) films increases the memory window (MW) beyond what is accounted for by the dielectric constants. Determining the physical mechanisms behind these MW improvements is critical to reaching the full potential of HZO FeNAND. Here, we show that MW improvements stem from the interfacial charge dynamics enabled by oxygen vacancies at the interlayer interface. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy(XPS) etching experiments demonstrate increased off-stoichiometry at the interface, with a 2.3x increase in oxygen vacancies. Polarization-dependent XPS and first-order reversal curves(FORC) show that tunneling between interfacial defect states causes a bidirectional internal bias of 0.56MV/cm. The impact of defects is further corroborated through phase-field modeling(PFM), which only recreates the coercive fields, FORC, and internal bias for defect densities and tunneling barrier heights that are consistent with experiment, quantitatively capturing an internal electric field of 0.55 MV/cm. The phase field models are then used to simulate 36 devices with varied charge densities and dielectric thickness to provide a predictive framework for further improvements in the MW of interlayer HZO. These findings redefine the role of defects in ferroelectric HZO from deleterious to engineerable and provide critical insights into how to tune ferroelectric device architectures for improved memory.
items.title: Tuning the Coercive Field in Ferroelectric Hf0.5Zr0.5O2-Al2O3 Heterostructures via Interfacial Charge Dynamics

items.summary: We introduce a Hankel--Christoffel--Nevai framework for screening posterior-relevant candidates in Bayesian inverse problems. A likelihood-weighted moment matrix records how Bayesian updating changes the geometry of the prior, and Christoffel and Nevai constructions convert this information into inexpensive relevance scores. The Christoffel ratio captures relative local moment mass, whereas the Nevai score provides a stable polynomially localized approximation of the likelihood. The moment matrix can be estimated from deterministic likelihood values, bounded unbiased marks, posterior samples, or binary unbiased likelihood observations. The construction extends to function-valued unknowns through nested feature maps, where the induced conditional likelihood has an exact Bayesian interpretation. We establish consistency and error bounds that separate feature resolution, polynomial localization, and pilot estimation. The same learned geometry can also be used to reorder exact stochastic likelihood blocks, reducing expected work without altering the posterior target. Numerical experiments on nonlinear, PDE-based, and function-space inverse problems demonstrate effective posterior-mass screening and computational savings.
items.title: Hankel-Christoffel-Nevai Screening of Posterior Relevance in Bayesian Inverse Problems

items.summary: A 3D city model is only as accurate as its building heights, and a model built from open data mostly infers those heights, from a mapped floor count, a height raster or a default value, rather than taking them from a mapped height. Maqueta reconstructs real places from open geospatial layers, with terrain from the Copernicus GLO-30 surface model, building footprints and roads from Overture Maps, water, green areas and rail from OpenStreetMap, population from GHS-POP, and building heights from the Google Open Buildings 2.5D raster where it has coverage, and it records for every building how its height was obtained. Across the 118 baked places and 4.05 million buildings, 8.8% of heights come from a mapped height attribute, 6.4% from a mapped floor count, 73.2% from the Open Buildings 2.5D height raster, itself a model estimate from satellite imagery, and 11.6% from a default prior of 8 m. A public LoD2 reference exists for two of the places, both in the Netherlands, where the raster has no coverage. Against the 3D BAG, the fused heights have a root-mean-square error of 3.1 m at Delft, with a bias of -0.1 m, and of 8.3 m at Amsterdam, with a bias of -6.6 m; the Amsterdam figure rests on 50 reference buildings. The raster heights, which supply most of the buildings, are not validated by this benchmark, and public ground truth for open-data building heights is scarce. Interactive tool and reproducible pipeline (MIT): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_RES_Maqueta . Fusion core: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_GeoScena .
items.title: Maqueta: Height Provenance in Open-Data 3D Urban Reconstruction Across 118 Places
